meta.title: The Cost of Making a Deal
meta.theme: why so much economic activity is organised by instruction inside firms rather than by prices in a market

format.format_verified: 2026-09: four-sentence TITA jumble, the modern CAT default; re-verify against each new official paper

meta.learning_objective: make a sentence beginning 'The reason is' explain the sentence it actually answers, and find the opener by what a sentence is owed rather than by which one lacks a definite article

quality.adversarial_review: The designed rival puts the sentence beginning 'The reason is' immediately after the opening claim about prices, because both sentences are about markets and prices and a definite article invites attachment to the nearest plausible antecedent. It fails twice. Read there, the sentence would be giving the reason why prices coordinate strangers well, when what it actually says is that using them is costly, which is close to the opposite. And the closing sentence speaks of 'those costs', which would then have nothing to point at, since the sentence before it names no costs at all. A second rival moves the definition of a firm up to third place and ends on the list of costs, which strands the same demonstrative. The third rival is new and the most instructive: every sentence in the set now opens on a definite phrase except the definition of a firm, so a solver applying the rule that the opener is the sentence with no backward reference will put the definition first. It is a good rule and it fails here, because the definition rests on 'those costs' and the costs are named in the sentence it would be standing in front of.

blind_solve.notes: First blind solve agreed with the key but reported that the first position could be fixed on sight, the opener being the only sentence in the set with no backward reference. Repaired by rewriting the opening proposition so that it too begins on a definite phrase, one whose reference is external, which leaves the indefinite definition of a firm looking like the natural opener while 'those costs' still forbids it. Awaits re-solve.

source.usage_note: Original composition in CAT register for CAT OS. General economics of firms and transaction costs; no specific text adapted or quoted. Personal study only.

meta.reviewer_notes: A cat-plus jumble built on definite articles. Three sentences now open with the — the proposition, the claim, the reason — and a fourth turns on a demonstrative pointing at costs; each points somewhere different, and only the first points outside the paragraph. Two decoys: a pair of sentences that share the vocabulary of markets and prices while answering different questions, and a definition of a firm that is the only sentence with an indefinite opening and therefore the one a solver's opener heuristic reaches for.

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: The reason is that using the market is itself expensive: finding a supplier, agreeing a price, writing a contract that anticipates what neither party can foresee.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: A firm is what appears wherever those costs exceed the cost of simply telling somebody what to do, and its boundary is drawn exactly there.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: The claim leaves an awkward fact unexplained: most of the work done in any economy is not coordinated by prices at all, but by instructions issued inside firms.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: The proposition economists reach for first is that prices coordinate strangers better than any planner could.

links.explanation: C opens 'The claim', a definite reference to the proposition D has just named, and then produces a fact that the proposition cannot account for. D's own definite phrase points outward, at a habit of economists, which is why D can stand first and C cannot.

A answers the awkward fact C has raised: work is organised by instruction because dealing through the market costs something. Read anywhere else, the sentence would be explaining why prices coordinate well, which is not what it says.

B speaks of 'those costs', and the costs are the three A has just listed: finding a supplier, agreeing a price, writing a contract against an unforeseeable future. The demonstrative fixes B immediately after A.

explanation.macro_pattern_note: The paragraph begins with a general proposition, produces the fact that embarrasses it, explains the fact, and then converts the explanation into a definition. It reads as a small piece of detective work, and like most detective work it cannot be reordered: the awkward fact must arrive before its explanation, and the definition must arrive after the thing it defines has been made necessary.

movement.label: D
movement.why_here: D opens on a definite phrase like most of the set, but its phrase reaches outside the paragraph, to what economists habitually say, and so needs nothing in front of it. It is also the proposition the rest of the paragraph qualifies, which is why it has to be first.

movement.label: C
movement.why_here: C is the turn, and its opening phrase names what it is turning against. It replaces the comfortable picture with a fact about where work is actually coordinated, and that fact is what the next sentence has to explain.

movement.label: A
movement.why_here: A explains C. Placed anywhere earlier it would appear to explain the coordinating power of prices, when what it reports is the cost of using them, and the paragraph would contradict itself at the second sentence.

movement.label: B
movement.why_here: B converts the explanation into a definition and closes. It is the only sentence here that opens indefinitely, which makes it look like an opener, but 'those costs' ties it to A's list, and a boundary drawn exactly there is the last thing the paragraph has to say.

tempting_orders.why_tempting: The sentence beginning 'The reason is' talks about markets, prices and suppliers, and so does the opening sentence. A definite article looks for the nearest antecedent it can use, and here the nearest one is available and on the same subject.
tempting_orders.where_it_breaks: In that seat the sentence gives the reason why prices coordinate strangers well, and what it actually says is that using them is expensive. The paragraph would be contradicting itself in two sentences. The closing sentence then strands too, since 'those costs' would point at a sentence about instructions inside firms, which names no costs.

tempting_orders.why_tempting: The list of costs is concrete and specific, and specific things make satisfying endings; the definition of a firm looks like a piece of theory that should be got out of the way as soon as the puzzle has been set.
tempting_orders.where_it_breaks: 'Those costs' has nothing to refer to when the list of costs comes after it. A demonstrative cannot point forwards, and the definition would be resting on an antecedent the reader has not yet been given.

tempting_orders.why_tempting: Every sentence in the set opens on a definite phrase except the definition of a firm, which begins with an indefinite article and reads like the first line of a textbook chapter. A solver who has learned that the opener is the sentence with no backward reference will take it, and the rest then arranges itself plausibly enough: the received view, the fact that embarrasses it, and the cost of dealing as the closing explanation.
tempting_orders.where_it_breaks: An indefinite article is not the same as independence. The definition contains 'those costs', a demonstrative whose members are the three items listed in the sentence about finding a supplier, agreeing a price and writing a contract, and in the first seat it points at nothing at all. The paragraph would also define a firm by a cost it has not yet described and then describe that cost at the end, which reverses its own explanation.

explanation.trap_named: The trap is the generic definite article, working at both ends of the paragraph. English uses 'the' both for things already named and for things known in general — the market, the firm, the proposition economists reach for — and a setter can exploit the ambiguity twice over: by writing a sentence whose 'the' looks like a backward reference to the nearest sentence on the same subject, and by making the true opener begin with 'the' as well, so that the one indefinite sentence looks like the natural start. The defence is the same in both places. Read what the sentence needs, not how it begins: a sentence opening 'The reason is' has to be a reason for something specific, and a sentence containing 'those costs' has to stand after the costs whatever its first article is.
explanation.solving_habit: For every sentence that opens with 'The reason', 'The claim' or 'The answer', state in your own words what question it answers, and then find the sentence that asks exactly that question. Then check the opener candidates the same way: go through each definite phrase and each demonstrative and ask whether a reader arriving cold could supply it. The sentence that is owed nothing is the opener, and it may well begin with 'the'.

mentor.challenge: Two sentences here are about markets and prices, and they must not be neighbours. One sentence looks like the opener because of a single article; check what it is owed before you believe it.
mentor.paragraph_plain: The proposition economists reach for first is that prices coordinate strangers better than any planner could manage. That leaves an uncomfortable fact unaccounted for: most work in any economy is not coordinated by prices at all, but by people inside firms being told what to do. The explanation is that using the market costs something in itself — you have to find a supplier, settle a price, and write a contract covering things neither side can predict. A firm is simply what appears wherever those costs are higher than the cost of giving an instruction, and that is exactly where its boundary lies.
mentor.takeaway: 'The reason is' must answer a question the paragraph has actually asked; and the opener is the sentence that is owed nothing, not the sentence that happens to begin with 'a'.
